No t e s
1. 
The Roth-Perry Two-Step, Roth and Perry are emphatic that the 
question whether due process “apphes” must be distinguished from, and 
answered prior to, the question of what process is due if due process is 
triggered. They also insist that interest balancing is not part of this threshold 
determination. The appeal of this analytic approach, however, is far from self- 
evident. In Cafeteria Workers, supra, the Court seemed to presume the 
apphcabihty of due process to Rachel Brawner’s employment claim and move 
directly to the question of to what sort of ‘Tiearmg^’ she was entitled. Although 
the answer in that case was “none,” the Court’s analysis was rooted entirely in 
its assessment of the competing interests involved. Are there reasons to prefer 
the more categorical approach of Roth-Perry7
2. 
Substantive Constitutional Rights as Procedurally Protected 
Interests. Professor Roth attributed the non-renewal of his contract to 
retaliation by his employer against Roth’s pubhc criticism of university 
administrators. Some such government employee criticism is, indeed, 
protected by the First Amendment, see Pickering v. Board of Education, 391 
U.S. 563 (1968), and the Supreme Court has recognized a constitutional right 
not to be fired for the exercise of First Amendment rights, see, e.g., Branti v. 
Finkel, 445 U.S. 507, 509 n. 3 (1980) (“[PJlaintiffs’ constitutional right * * * is 
the right not to be dismissed from pubhc employment upon the sole ground of 
their pohtical beliefs.”). Protection of First Amendment interests extends to 
independent contractors as weU. See, e.g., Bd. ofCnty Comm'rs v. Umbehr, 518 
U.S. 668 (1996); O'Hare Truck Service v. Northlake, 518 U.S. 712 (1996).
If Roth’s claim is at least colorable, why is the First Amendment right he 
asserts not a liberty interest that can support a procedural claim for a due 
process hearing? Would an administrative hearing on his non-renewal have 
served any value, given the availabihty of a judicial forum in which to test 
Roth’s claim?
